title: Reading Between the Lines
blurb: Guess the meaning of new words from context

steps.html:
On one Spanish island, a conversation can cross a valley without a single word being spoken. Two texts, a set of verbs that insist on their own preposition, and a way of dealing with words you have never seen.

  • Work out the meaning of new words from the text around them
  • Use consist of, contribute to, adapt to, result in and others
  • Write a short description of a way of communicating

steps.title: Text A · A language made of whistles
steps.html:
Written for this course, from the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage listing for Silbo Gomero (2009).

Most travellers have never heard of La Gomera, and those who have usually know it for one extraordinary thing. The island is the worn tip of an old volcano, cut through by ravines so deep and slopes so steep that two farms facing each other across a valley can be an hour apart on foot. Long before there were roads, the islanders solved that problem by learning to whistle their language across it.

Silbo Gomero is not a code, and it is not a set of agreed signals for danger or dinner. It consists of a small set of whistled sounds that stand for the vowels and consonants of ordinary Spanish: two whistles carry all five vowels, four more carry the consonants, and the ear separates them by pitch and by whether the sound is continuous or broken. Because the system consists of sounds rather than of ready-made messages, and maps onto the language itself, anything an islander can say, an islander can whistle. A skilled whistler is understood two or three kilometres away, across country that would take most of a morning to cross. At that distance, with the wind moving, visitors regularly mistake it for birdsong.

Nobody is certain where it came from. Most accounts point to North Africa, and when Spanish replaced the older island tongue the whistle was simply adapted to the new language and carried on, as it adapts to any change in the speech around it. It belonged, for ages, to shepherds and to anyone else whose working day was spent on a hillside. It has one built-in weakness: a whistled signal contains far less information than a spoken one, so the same whistle can correspond to several different words. That ambiguity results in genuine mistakes, and whistlers deal with it the way readers deal with a difficult sentence — by repeating, and by relying on context.

steps.title: Text B · Nearly lost, then legislated back
steps.html:
Written for this course, from the UNESCO listing (2009) and Carreiras, López, Rivero & Corina, Nature 433 (2005).

By the middle of the twentieth century Silbo was in trouble. Roads, telephones and emigration all contributed to its decline, and it acquired a reputation as something rural and backward. Plenty of islanders disapproved of it, and a good number were embarrassed by it: it belonged, they felt, to the poverty their children were escaping. Visitors who had heard of it expected folklore — a ukulele in a hotel lobby, a performance for tourists rather than a working language. By the 1980s the last fluent whistlers were mostly old men.

What rescued it was not enthusiasm but policy. In 1999 the island authorities made Silbo a compulsory subject in every primary and secondary school on La Gomera, and that decision has resulted in something no earlier attempt achieved: a whole generation that grew up whistling in class. In 2009 UNESCO added Silbo Gomero to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, describing it as the only whistled language in the world that is fully developed and practised by a large community — on an island of some 22,000 people.

The most interesting evidence, though, came from a laboratory. In 2005 a team led by Manuel Carreiras published a study in Nature that scanned the brains of fluent whistlers while they listened to Silbo. In those whistlers, the regions that normally handle speech responded to the whistles exactly as they respond to words. In Spanish speakers who could not whistle, the same sounds resulted in nothing of the kind: the brain filed them as noise. Language, it turns out, does not depend on the mouth. It adapts to whatever channel the landscape leaves open.

steps.title: Why the preposition is not optional
steps.html:
A recycled area. The full picture first, then a long example bank.

Some verbs are followed by a fixed preposition. The preposition is not chosen by meaning — it belongs to the verb, and there is usually no rule to work it out from. Learn the verb and its preposition as one item.

After these prepositions, a verb takes -ing, never the infinitive: She apologised for being late. — not for to be late.

Some verbs take a different preposition with a different meaning: hear of = know that something exists; hear about = get news of it; hear from = receive a message from someone.

A few verbs take an object first: adapt something to something — The locals adapted the language to Spanish.

steps.title: Building a sentence around a dependent preposition
steps.html:
1. You want to say that mobile phones were one cause of the decline.
  2. Choose the verb: contribute. Its preposition is fixed: to.
  3. Put the cause first, the preposition next, the result after it: Mobile phones contributed to the decline.
  4. If the result is an action rather than a noun, it must be -ing: Mobile phones contributed to killing the language. — never to kill here.
  5. Compare the stronger verb: result in claims a direct consequence, so Mobile phones resulted in the decline is a bigger claim than contributed to.

steps.title: Write your description.
steps.sub: 130–160 words. Use at least four verb + preposition pairs from this lesson.
steps.placeholder: Almost nobody outside … has heard of …
steps.html:
• Say what it is and what it consists of.
  • Explain what contributed to its decline, and what that resulted in.
  • Say how people feel about it now — who approves, who disapproves.
  • Finish with the situation today.

Useful language

  • It consists of …
  • … contributed to its decline.
  • … resulted in …
  • Older speakers disapprove of …
  • Younger people have adapted to …
  • Most people outside the region have never heard of it.
steps.modelHtml:
The whistled shepherds' calls of the mountains

Almost nobody outside the region has heard of them. The system consists of about twenty short calls, each one carrying a single instruction, and it was used by shepherds working on hills too steep to cross quickly.

Two things contributed to its decline. Roads reached the high pastures in the 1970s, and the radio arrived a decade later. Together they resulted in a generation that never needed to learn it.

A few older shepherds still disapprove of the recordings that researchers now make, because a call learned from a machine is not the same as a call learned on a hillside. Their grandchildren have adapted to the recordings anyway. Around forty people can still use the calls, which is thirty-nine more than in 1995.
